Messages.Author: Brian
Messages.Body:
I am primarily a competitive player. As such, I don't really know
what casual players are thinking. Still, lion cubs play rough, right?
It's a no-pressure simulation of what they might face later in their
life. I think that's what a person's playgroup should be like.

I'm trying to figure out what makes a person choose casual play or
competitive play over the other. So far, I think one factor is,
tournaments are all about winning. Those of us who feel pressured by
that will more likely play casually, right?

I love to lose. I never have so much inspiration to build a new deck,
or change an existing one, as when I get utterly creamed in a good
game. I think this is what makes me such a competitive player, as
anyone who can't take losing may just take their focus off of it
altogether.

Anyone have any opinions about this? Why do you play the way you do?

There are many factors as to why some play in tournaments and others don't.
For some, it is the deck types that they know they will face in a tournament
(the cheese & sleaze argument). For some, they may not like meeting or
playing with new people they haven't met socially first. And for others,
they may not necessarily need to win, but they don't want to be crushed in
the first 3 turns. They just want to play.

In my personal experience, tournaments (especially big convention ones) are
all about meeting fabulous players and people from all over. Meeting people
whose posts you've read on the infamous newsgroup. Trying to figure out
whether you could beat up Derek Ray in real life. And they are a blast. Of
course, unlike your average gamer, I don't suffer discomfort in social
situations. I can talk to a pretty girl without having to change my
underwear afterwards.

> I love to lose. I never have so much inspiration to build a new deck,
> or change an existing one, as when I get utterly creamed in a good
> game. I think this is what makes me such a competitive player, as
> anyone who can't take losing may just take their focus off of it
> altogether.

I disagree. I think players who can take losing are more apt to play in
casual environments. Players who "can't take losing" aren't in it for a
"good game". Really, it's the old power gamer v. social gamer argument.

Players who hate to lose either won't or don't have fun (meaning by choice
or by genetics? nature v. nurture?) when they are losing. If they are losing
because the metagame (the archetypes and unique characteristics of the decks
that players are fielding) doesn't favor them, they will either try to
change the metagame or stop playing.

Of course, changing the metagame is favorable to reducing the number of
available players in a playgroup. But what if the deck type required to
change the metagame is one that you hate playing?

The thing about this game is that you can build a deck that won't win
without insuring that someone else will. You can build a deck that won't
oust your prey, but will prevent them from playing (thank you HoS, to name
one archetype. Too bad it isn't spelt "Skulles", because I think "HoSe" is
more appropriate.) How do you change the metagame away from these deck
types?

> Anyone have any opinions about this? Why do you play the way you do?

I used to play to make people laugh. Then I played to win. Then I played to
play. Now it's just not worth it if someone (not even the same person every
time) is going to be furious at the end of every game.

-Mike Ooi

To me, this is a strange question when asked in the context of Jyhad. Every
place I've played, I see all the same guys playing tournaments that are in my
casual play groups. The atmosphere seems the same as the casual games I play.
There's maybe a little more adherence to technical rules. For instance, you
get into your turn without taking the edge pool, you're just stuck whereas in
a casual game you can take it and no one really bothers you about it. But
for the most part, I barely notice the difference. Even in the large
tournaments I've been going to in Los Angeles this past year are fine.
Everyone's cordial, no one seems to have any problems with anyone else for the
most part, and the lesser experienced players meld in just fine (albeit they
don't necessarily win much).

Magic was completely different in this respect. I stopped playing big Magic
tournaments for a lot of reasons but one of the main ones was that everyone
was so uptight about everything. Besides complete and absolute adherence to
all the sticky technical rules and jokers trying to argue with you about
minutia, you'd run into poor sports and hotshots with attitudes and people who
thought "jedi mind tricks" were cute and just all sorts of boorish behavior.
I found myself being irritable and overreactive from the environment I was in
and it probably reflected in my own behavior towards others. The funny thing
was that I found Magic boring outside of tournaments for the most part since
too many people wouldn't take casual play seriously enough to make the play
interesting. (Too many dumb trick decks and stuff.) I found the best niche
was the local store tournaments where most everyone knew each other too well
to behave uncivilly (after all, they would see each other again next week)
but were serious enough to play to win. I might still be playing Magic that
way if WotC didn't insist on their three expansions per year schedule.

Fred

>>I'm still not completely sure about tournaments. Though I've been posting on

tournaments fairly recently. My first two tournaments or so (last year) left a

I gotta say that I find that odd. I don't play in a huge number of tournaments
or anything, but I play at Origins every year, a few larger tournaments around
the Northeast every year, and multiple smallish local events every year, and I
find that tournament VTES players are quite personable and fun to play with.
Sure, people are often much more sticklers to the actual rules (like missing
out on taking pool for having the edge), but I have rarely run across people
being psychos about stuff like that. The last two really big tournaments I
played--Origins and the Northeast Quallifier both had very friendly
competetors, and I can't remember any disputes over rules or game
play--everyone was pretty chill. Certainly the small local events that tend to
be made of people from three fairly close playgroups (that we see fairly often)
are all very relaxed, even if we are playing for prizes.

>>Once you start having people demand you can't get Edge pool once you're in
your Master phase, you have other such nit-picks.>>

I'm not quite sure what other such nit-picks there are. Getting blood from the
edge is optional--if you don't take it at the right point in the turn, you are
effectively opting not to take it. Sure, in casual play (and even in
competetive play) I personally wouldn't care, and would let someone get blood
from the edge if they forgot, but that is me, and I can certainly understand
people wanting to play by the fairly strict enforcement of the rules,
especially if money (i.e. prizes) are involved.

>>*All* the little nitty-gritty details are enforced because they might give
some player a little bit of an edge. So overall, I found normal tournaments to
have a bit of a hostile environment.>>

I don't think they are enforced 'cause they might give someone a bit of an
edge--they are enforced 'cause they are the rules, and if you are playing
competetively (i.e. where something is at stake--prizes, ratings,
quallifiaction for another event, whatever), it is best that the rules get
enforced. This doesn't mean that someone has to be a dick about it, no, but it
is probably best to assume that rules (even small ones) will be strictly
enforced in a competetive setting--that the default understanding is that
everyone will be playing by the same strict rules, rather than assuming that
everyone will be playing with the same casual outlook that you or I might have.

All this being said, however, I still have had pretty much nothing but good
experiences at VTES tournaments, and find that the vast bulk of competetive
VTES players are very nice, cordial, and fun to play with. Sure, there is the
occasional idiot or ass, but they are far fewer and further between than not.

I have a bit of a different take on the strict adherence to the rules. I
believe its much friendlier to play with the strict adherence. When you think
about it, there's less to argue about. If you typically allow people to take
the edge pool and hunting grounds, etc. during their master phase, you'll
inevitably run into a situation where someone at your tournament says "Hey, you
already took blood from your hunting ground" or "you already gained a pool for
the edge!". Not only that, but if you are going to allow take-backs and other
exceptions to the rules, you'll eventually find situations that cannot be taken
back "Oh, wait! I should have gained the edge last turn and I forgot to take
it! So, I'm not ousted afterall!". Clearly, there is some point in which
you're going to say that too much time has passed. Problem is, people will draw
the line differently at where that line will be drawn. Then you open the door
to claims of favortism ("The judge always let's his own playgroup do it!").
Ugh. Anyway, in small casual groups you can oftentimes work out most of the
details and begin to think similarly about where to draw the line and how to
judge these murky areas. This minimizes or eliminates the arguments. When you
are playing with 30 strangers it makes much more sense to officially draw the
line in the same way.

As Peter said though, people shouldn't use the strict adherence as an excuse to
be a jerk.

> In addition, another factor might be that I've gradually gotten to know some
of
> the people who play at the tournaments. So perhaps a tournament may seem
> hostile when you don't know anyone there, but as you gradually get to know
> them, the very seem atmosphere drastically changes.

In some games, playeres are essentially playing multiplayer solitaire. When my
kids play Candyland, they make their way to the finish with no interaction
between players. Victory in V:TES *requires* you to achieve your win on the
corpses of your opponents. Games like V:TES are naturally more difficult to
play with strangers. The tendency would almost be to want to apologize after
torporizing the stranger's vamps. :) Getting to know people certainly makes it
easier.

-Robert

Fred wrote:
>>All very good points. However, as you make them you have to understand that

tournaments as a more hostile environment, when in fact this is just the way

Which I agree with, but am constantly confused by. Tournaments are places where
folks go to play and win stuff--they are playing for money, prizes, bragging
rights, whatever. In any game, whenever people play for something, rules tend
to be strictly enforced, be it high school basketball, bridge, darts, or VTES.
When people are playing for money, everyone likes to make sure that everyone is
on the up and up. Playing by a strict adherence to the rules is the best way to
do this.

I guess where folks get confused is when they don't understand the difference
between adhering to the rules and being a prick, as it is perfectly possible to
adhere to the rules strictly without being a prick, and most people I have
played tournament VTES with have been not pricks, while we all are pretty good
about strict adherence to the rules.

>>I only bring this up since the focal point of the thread seems like it's
really more about how people perceive the tournament environment than the
justification for strict adherence to the rules.>>

The perception comes from, I'd figure, the assumption that people at a
tournament are going to be completely laid back and just as flexible about the
rules as your home play group, rather than the assumption that people at a
tournament are going to strictly adhere to the rules, and expect that everyone
do that.

As I mentioned elsewhere, it seems likely that if everyone went to a tournament
assuming that the default will be "strict adherence to rules" rather than "laid
back and flexible adherence to the rules", everyone would be much happier.

Just like if everyone went to a VTES tournament with the default assumption
"everyone will be playing very effective decks that are going to do their best
to kill me" rather than "everyone will be playing goofy, role-playing, theme
decks, and will be just as amused as me when I play my all Werewolf pack deck".
Kind of like when you go to a chess tournament, you'll automatically assume "my
opponents are going to do their best to check mate me", where you won't
automatically assume "my opponents will be unconcerened with actually trying to
check mate me, but instead will be doing everything in their power to kill my
Bishops above all other goals".

If they're catching every action you do, either play more stealth than
they can catch, or unblockable actions (seduction + CotHD works well).

Casual vs. competitive:

I guess I'm more of a casual player, so I'll try to offer my
perspective.

I like to play games, but even moreso, I like to design (decks,
characters, worlds, etc.). This probably stems from my being the only
person I knew growing up who actually read the rules to the games,
which meant that I could generally beat anyone else whom I could
convince to play; the real issue was not winning, but rather
convincing people to play, and then to play again. And when I
couldn't do that, I'd play with myself <insert smiley thing here>,
which is to say I'd design characters/worlds, or play decks/sides
against each other, etc. for my own entertainment.

Anyway, it is not sufficient for me to win; winning with a stock S&B
deck bores me and makes me want to apologize to the other players for
my lack of creativity. (It was the first deck I built, and, yes, I
did actually think I was pretty clever to have come up with S&B until
I realized that everyone else had too... Vote pushing would have been
my next design triumph.) It seems too easy. (Given the vagaries of
seating order in V:TES, of course, it's not really that easy... I'm
generalizing across games here.) I'm much more interested in finding
novel ways to win (Thus the editorship of the !Ventrue Newsletter -
I'll let people know if I make a breakthrough...), and in enjoying the
interaction of the cards and players.

I do play to win, but I don't play _in order to_ win. I play because
I like problem solving and interacting with other people in ways that
exercise our brains/imagination. I have a hard time understanding why
someone would play just to win - what possible life goal could that
person be satisfying? (Step 143 of program of world domination:
Establish mastery of Jyhad...)

> The incompatibility between these two styles (in reality, it is more a
> spectrum between) creates a layer of frustration and tension between players
> that can lead to hurt feelings, etc. In short, it can kill a playgroup. It
> killed ours.

I can certainly see how that might be true. The massive influx of
'competitive' players to Magic: The Garnishing was a big part of why
I stopped playing it. I mean, when the official magazines are
publishing articles on how to 'psych your opponents out and win more
games', it's time (for me, at least) to move on.

> The Austin playgroup is dead.

Bogus. On the bright side, now that I actually have no time to play
(and am planning to move to Seattle), the Chicago playgroup(s) seem to
be reviving...

> Hell, I'm inventorying my cards right now for a big run on Ebay.
> (Okay, there are other factors invovled. But exaggeration for emphasis...)

I've certainly thought about doing this myself more than once, and may
still get around to it. (Though I already have them inventoried -
thanks Dave & Sorrow.)

> > competitive play over the other. So far, I think one factor is,
> > tournaments are all about winning. Those of us who feel pressured by
> > that will more likely play casually, right?

Why I played in tournaments: I had no other choice (other than not
playing at all). There was no playgroup in my area, or at least not
one that I could get to. Tournaments were the only avenue for me to
play. Had I had a choice, I'm not sure I wouldn't have played in
tournaments as well as casually, but I think it's important to keep in
mind that for isolated players, a well advertised nearby tournament
scene may be their only opportunity.

> There are many factors as to why some play in tournaments and others don't.
> For some, it is the deck types that they know they will face in a tournament
> (the cheese & sleaze argument). For some, they may not like meeting or
> playing with new people they haven't met socially first. And for others,
> they may not necessarily need to win, but they don't want to be crushed in
> the first 3 turns. They just want to play.

I'd have to say that learning to play in tournaments was a really,
really bad way to do it in my experience. Personal mistakes (#1) and
seating order (#2) decided practically every game I played. It was
frustrating enough when other people were patient; when they were
jerks it was so intolerable that I nearly quit playing altogether.

Of course, since my all tournament, all the time intro to the game,
I've managed to play a few 'casual' games, and they have been, if
anything, worse, by and large. There's nothing like spending an hour
each way fighting traffic to spend three hours playing two games, both
of which go like this:

Player 1 (turn two): ...and four transfers brings up Devin!

Player 5 (preying on 1): Dammit! You're not playing that deck again?

Player 1: Yep.

Player 5: Well, I can't win then. I'll make a deal with you...
(Proceeds to make deal whereby he not only hoses himself, but also his
grandprey - me.)

Player A (drawing initial crypt): Well, I can't win.

Player A (later in game): Why am I cross-tabling? I'm hosed, so I
thought I'd just help out other people who are in trouble. (Proceeds
to help own predator.)

Other people's familiarity (with each others' decks) certainly breeds
my contempt. If the game wasn't so darn well-designed, and so many of
the players weren't such, well, non-gamerish people, I'd have dropped
it long ago.

> In my personal experience, tournaments (especially big convention ones) are
> all about meeting fabulous players and people from all over. Meeting people
> whose posts you've read on the infamous newsgroup. Trying to figure out
> whether you could beat up Derek Ray in real life. And they are a blast.

tournaments are competitive. i don't agree with this premise - i find

players, for diverse reasons such as uneven player ability, weird
table dynamics and incompatibility of different metagames. i play in
tournaments not for the competition but because i believe it's the
best way to promote the game, so i'm always a little bit detached in
such an environment.

Given the choice i would always opt for a GENUINELY competitive game,
which means players of equal ability playing decent decks that are all
capable of showing what they can do in the environment provided by the
other decks. Sometimes you get this in tournaments. At home i create a
library of decks that are reasonably well-balanced vis-a-vis one
another, and to equalise the playing field i allow guests and family
to CHOOSE a deck, while i pick randomly from the ones that are left.
But perhaps the best game in which i've played recently was at Rob's
house when we were:

Me, playing my Brit-combo deck [NOT the one i posted, the one i played
was MUCH better], bleeding
Rob, playing an Anneke/ToGP deck, bleeding
Jon Cooper, playing a massive Malkavian takeover deck, bleeding
Pierre, who was abusing the !Nosferatu library depletion cards,
bleeding
Barney, who was playing Assamites with the Succubus club.

This was i suppose a friendly game and much beer was drunk, but the
level of play was EXTRAORDINARILY high, and i've NEVER seen so many
heart-breakingly powerful cards played, nor evil deals proposed and
accepted, in a game. After about 3 hours of slaughter we decided that
it was going to be a 2-all draw between me and Barney because the two
of us were reduced to conspiring through the Succubus club to prevent
Jon from getting the remaining 3 VP, and he was a bit bored by that
prospect. Come to think of it we played two more games after that,
both equally good [i think i won one with Malkavian ToGP, and lost the
other with Rafastio Ghouls a gogo [Barney won IIRC]], before an
alcoholic haze descended upon our faculties and Lady Legbiter arrived
to take me home. In comparison, the tournament the next day was a bit
tame, really.

i've had equally good competitive games whilst visiting my SE USA
friends and we occasionally get a REALLY good game down the pub on
Wednesday night. So i suppose what i am saying is that people who
dislike playing in tourneys may, actually, be pining for a GENUINELY
competitive game, which they find is not afforded them by that
environment.

Well, for me its a variety of reasons why I abhor current competitive
(tournament) play and stick to casual gaming.

First, I play Jyhad to be entertained and to entertain. Not every deck
that is not stealth bleed or weenie potence is a "all werewolf pack
deck" or "try and kill your bishops." I like to experiment with new
deck styles and discipline/clan combinations. I like to play against a
variety of deck styles and players, and to use new deck styles myself.

I went to the NA qualifier last year and saw carbon copy decks.
Ventrue Bleed and Bloat. Eurobrujah bleed and bloat. Weenie presence.
Weenie potence. Standard archtypes. I just dont gain a lot of joy out
of playing against netdecks.

Further, a lot of people play in tournaments specifically to meet new
people and play against different playstyles than their local game.
They sit down at a tourney table and are very likely to see the same
deckstyle at table one as they see at table 2 as they see at table
three, and thats not entertaining.

To people like me, Jyhad is a game played for enjoyment. Enjoyment is
not gained by winning prizes or beating opponents alone. Enjoyment for
me (and I'll bet many others who play the casual game) is gained by
doing your best and playing with nice blokes who are willing to be
creative in deck design as well as play. Tournament Jyhad is generally
not the place to find this.

I love playing casual Jyhad with Jay from Columbus. However, look at
his tourney deck choices... very different from sitting down with Jay
over a casual game, and that difference is why I eschew Tourney level
Jyhad. People feel they need to ramp it up to be competitive, and
creativity in deck design is what often gets sacrificed to meet that
end.

Where Peter is dead nuts on is that rules enforcement should be
strictly expected at any table, casual or tourney. However, when you
remind someone of something they missed be kind about it. DO NOT jump
up, point, dance and shout "You screwed up you screwed up." (I am not
exaggerating. This happened to me at a tournament).

Matt

Who cares?!? That's kind of the whole point of experimenting, I think.
I'm wondering who cares if your bizarre X deck works wonderfully against
other players' bizarre decks Y, Z, and so forth but falls flat on its face
against any serious, normal tournament decks?

In Major League Baseball's spring training (Grapefruit and Cactus) leagues,
there's an unwritten rule that addresses this same issue. In spring training,
besides the regular players, teams also invite a number of high minor leaguers
in order to evaluate them in major league play. The trouble is, if both teams
only field minor leaguers in their lineup, they don't get evaluated in a major
league game. It's essentially just another triple-A game, which the teams
can test their players in all year. So the unwritten rule is that each team
must keep at least four legitimate major league players on the field/in the
lineup at all times so the other team can get an adequate evaluation of where
their players are at.

I feel the same way about Jyhad. I'm not going to force anyone in a pickup
game to play a serious deck (after all, if my deck is an experiment, why
not theirs?). But I'm sure not going to discourage it, either.

will destroy the table. The Weenie Presence deck will clearly win the
table.

developmental stages, ie never be tier one. There are a whole slew of
decks that, while they cannot beat a table with Eurobrujah, Ventrue
Bloat, weenie potence and Malk S/B, they may be competitive against an
Ahrimanes deck, a Lasombra bruise and bleed, a Giovanni theft deck,
and Toreador with guns.

In short, some deck designs will never qualify for further testing
against a serious gauntlet, and hence never be tourney worthy. But
casual games allow those fun, strange concepts to have a home. Casual
games are a place where every deck has a chance.

#2 is the big, gaping flaw in the whole concept. I think a lot of people
_want_ certain kinds of neat, concept decks they've figured out to work.
The trouble is, they won't work in a tournament environment or at the very
least need a lot of tuning. So you come up with this idea for a "nut-puncher"
game or, as Wes calls it, a "deck-lab" game. Let's call a spade a spade
here, though: we're talking about playing games with weak decks so that other
people with weak decks can have a chance. The trouble is, there's no play-
balance in an environment with such deckbuilding rules because the deckbuilding
rules aren't laid out in an understandable way. Everyone's definition of
"weak" varies. People can't be sure if their deck is "weak enough" to conform
to the standard because there's no objective standard. That's why we have
deckbuilding rules and designers who focus on designing, banning, and errataing
the environment - so that the environment is balanced.

I suppose if you get a group of players who are pretty good at eyeballing a
deck and figuring if it's about right for the unwritten standards of the
environment, it might not work out too bad. To me, it doesn't seem like a
very worthwhile exercise because I can't figure out what winning and losing
means in an environment like that. If you just want to experience some kind
of unusual and remarkable effect in the game - say, a minion with 7 Raptors
or something of that nature - then perhaps this would appeal to you. That
just doesn't spin my buttons, personally.

Fred

Something in here made me recall something about evaluating decks. When I play
a new deck, I don't rate it on results. Too many times I've seen horrible
decks win individual games. It has to play 3+ games for results to become
meaningful. What I do rate it on is how smooth card flow is and how often it
does what it's supposed to and whether what it's supposed to be doing is in any
way effective.

In experimental games, you will at least get some idea of these. You won't
know whether you have the resilience or firepower to deal with tournament
decks, but often, you will figure out some of the necessary tuning to make a
deck better.

In a tournament game, you may very well get pounded too fast to see how your
cards interact and figure out what should be replaced. You will eventually
want to put a deck up against stiff competition, but if that's all you do, you
may miss out on possible lines of development.

From what I've seen, it's a common problem for players to not have fun when
they don't approach the game the same way. As long as everyone is on the same
page, fun can be had regardless as to what the rules are, the card pool is
like, or whatever. But, not everyone is amenable to being on the same page.

Fixes? Don't know. The various suggestions have sounded reasonable. For one
of my CCG groups (not V:TES), I tried suggesting all sorts of possibilities
from variant formats to time limits to house rules to just trying to figure out
what people liked and didn't like. None of it worked. Should note that there
were far fewer problems when we had more players as any individual's exposure
to what they found undesirable was lessened.

I'm kind of surprised though that it has become a problem, in other words, that
it wasn't a problem before but is now. I suppose people's styles can evolve
over time. And, it is true that card pools evolve over time in ways that some
may find less fun. Also, it can be the case that card pools don't evolve
enough to keep a game fresh. Hmm. Maybe, it isn't so surprising.

Does everyone realize there's a problem? If not, that's part of the problem.
If that's out of the way, the various suggestions can be tried.
